newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open a bit lower before jobless data.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open a bit lower before jobless data.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices opened unchanged to narrowly lower on Monday as players adopted a more tentative stance before weekly jobless claims figures due within the hour and the January employment report due Friday.

Concerns about the January payrolls report, about supply coming in next week's $39.75 billion Treasury refunding operation, and a need to step back from what some strategists described as the market's "overbought" condition restrained prices, analysts said.
In early dealings, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was down 1/32 to 96-22/32, yielding 6.76 percent.

The market gets jobless claims data for the week ended February 1 at 0830 EST/1330 GMT. Claims are forecast to have fallen to 347,000 in the latest week from 351,000 a week earlier, according to a Reuters poll.

"Continuing claims are also important to look at this week because they dropped a lot the week of January 11 and those who look at the details in this report are waiting for it to move back up to what it had been averaging which is above 2,500,000," said I.D.E.A. senior bond strategist Josh Stiles.
Economists say weekly new jobless claims in the neighborhood of 345,000 are consistent with a payrolls trend of 200,000 a month job growth.

"The (January) payroll number is very much on the market's mind today," said Stiles. "There are rumors flying around that the payroll number wil be dramatically depressed by bad weather in the Midwest in January. And there are other rumors that it will be very strong.
"The range of estimates on payroll growth -- from 100,000 new jobs to over 400,000 -- is huge," said Stiles. "You could drive a truck through it."
Upcoming supply is also a concern. The Treasury will sell $39.75 billion in new three- 10- and 30-year securities next week in its quarterly refinancing operation.

"How that goes will be very heavily influenced by the payrolls data tomorrow," said Stiles. "If we got a friendly payrolls number on Friday, then the market would price securiites up and then we'd still have new concerns about how the auctions will go."
From a technical point of view, the market has come "a long way from the oversold conditions of a week ago and we've backed off from the 6-point straight up bounce," said Stiles.
"The market is neither heavily oversold and no longer heavily overbought," he said. "The market will probably stay in this area until tomorrow's payroll number."
Three- and six-month Treasury bill rates were unchanged at 4.99 percent and 5.07 percent, respectively. Year bill rates were up one basis point to 5.24 percent.
Two-year notes were down 1/32 to 99-20/32, yielding 5.91 percent. Five-year and 10-year notes were also unchanged at 100-24/32 and 100-7/32, respectively, yielding 6.22 percent and 6.47 percent.
